summary: Kasei is a tamagotchi-style Mars outpost survival game for kids aged 7 to 12 that runs in any phone or desktop browser, with no download or account. Players keep an outpost alive by spending limited Energy and Manpower on four systems: life support, power, radiation shielding and food. Because resources are shared, no choice is free, which is the real trade-off at the heart of the challenge. When a player ends the day, that Martian day's real radiation, temperature, pressure and sunlight from NASA's Curiosity rover hit the outpost. This archived data (not live) comes from the RAD and REMS instruments, and the game credits it on screen. A robot mascot, Kasei, shows how the outpost is doing, and an "Ask Kasei" helper explains terms like sol and radiation dose in plain words, using the same data. It matters because kids rarely see the decisions behind a mission, only the outcome. Kasei lets them feel those decisions, and learn from failing, in two minutes.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Kasei is a tamagotchi-style Mars outpost survival game for kids aged 7 to 12. Instead of a digital pet, the player keeps a whole outpost alive. Each turn is one sol (a Martian day). Four systems start at 100%: Life Support, Power, Radiation Shield and Food Production. Players have limited, shared Energy and Manpower, and each repair costs a different mix of both, so they cannot fix everything. When they end the day, that sol's real conditions from NASA's Curiosity rover are applied: more radiation wears the shield faster, and colder nights strain life support. A plain-language cause line explains what happened. A robot mascot, Kasei, shows the outpost's health through animated expressions that follow the weakest system. An "Ask Kasei" helper answers preset questions (What's a sol? Where does this data come from?) using the real data and current game state, so every answer is traceable. A history chart shows how each choice added up, and Undo lets players take back a move.

REAL NASA DATA

Radiation dose from Curiosity's RAD instrument (Heber & Löwe 2026) and temperature, pressure and sunlight from its REMS weather station (NASA Planetary Data System), sols 1500 to 1513. The data is archived, not live, and the game says so. The processing scripts are in our repository so judges can check the numbers.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Kids see the decisions behind a mission, not only its outcome. They learn that in space nothing is free, that ignoring radiation today causes problems tomorrow, and that failing is part of learning. It runs in a browser or on a phone with no download or account, so a teacher can run a whole mission between lessons.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Godot 4 (GDScript) for the game, exported to the web (GitHub Pages and itch.io). Python and PowerShell for downloading and processing the NASA data. Figma for the visual layout. Space Mono and Orbitron fonts.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Mars survival is turned into a pet-care game, so a 7-year-old understands an engineering trade-off through a friendly character. Fatima Mahzabin drew Kasei with two-frame animations for six moods. The chart tells its four lines apart by line style, not only colour.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Plain language for explaining sol and radiation dose, a portrait layout that scales to any screen, honest labelling of archived data, and a small palette for readability.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

The game replays one 14-sol window. Next we would use real solar-particle spikes from the same radiation record as new missions, add Earth-Mars communication delay, and make the Power trade-off respond more strongly to sunlight.
dataRefs: NASA MSL Curiosity REMS (Rover Environmental Monitoring Station) calibrated data, PDS Atmospheres Node, sols 1500-1513, “Air temperature (night low and daytime high), pressure and hours of sunlight for each sol. Archived data.”

NASA MSL Curiosity RAD (Radiation Assessment Detector) dose rates, processed by Heber & Löwe (2026), Zenodo, “Daily radiation dose in mGy per day, which sets how fast the radiation shield wears down. Archived data.”
